record.name: ReVita Water
record.about: ReVita Water was founded in 2014 by a small group of process engineers who spent years installing wastewater systems for large utilities and decided there was a better way to serve mid-sized industrial clients. We design, build, and commission compact wastewater treatment units for food processing and pharmaceutical manufacturing plants across the region. Our core product is the ReVita MBR unit — a membrane bioreactor system we size and configure for each client's flow rate, load, and discharge permit. We also offer multi-year service contracts that cover scheduled maintenance, membrane replacement, and remote PLC monitoring. Our team of 27 includes process engineers, automation technicians, a lab analyst, and field service crews. We are headquartered at NTP Novi Sad, where our small R&D lab lets us run pilot tests before committing to full installations. Clients include dairy cooperatives, soft-drink bottlers, a generics pharmaceutical manufacturer, and a cosmetics plant. What sets us apart is that we do not sell off-the-shelf units — every system is engineered to the client's actual loading data, and our service contracts mean we stay involved long after commissioning. We are currently developing a pharma-grade treatment line that targets trace pharmaceutical compounds, aiming for market readiness by 2028.

challenges.text: A pharmaceutical client must remove drug residues (diclofenac, carbamazepine) that our biological step doesn't catch.
challenges.detail: One of our pharmaceutical clients — a generics manufacturer in Sremska Mitrovica — must meet a discharge limit for active pharmaceutical ingredients before their permit renewal in late 2026. Right now our MBR system handles the biological oxygen demand fine, but two compounds keep showing up above the limit in effluent samples: diclofenac and carbamazepine. Both are well-known hard-to-degrade molecules, and our standard aerobic biology simply does not break them down enough. We have done some reading on ozonation and activated carbon polishing, but we have no in-house experience with either. Our process engineer ran a small-scale ozone contact test last autumn and got inconsistent results — partial removal some days, almost none others. We suspect the matrix is interfering but we do not know why. Our lab can measure the compounds by HPLC if we send samples to an external lab, which costs money and takes a week. Budget for a technical study is modest — around 15 000 EUR — and we cannot afford a large pilot rig without external co-funding. A good outcome would be a validated small-scale method we can build into a compact polishing stage that fits within the existing footprint at that client's site.

challenges.text: Membranes in dairy plants foul quickly and need cleaning every week.
challenges.detail: At two dairy plants we service — one near Temerin, one outside Bečej — our MBR membranes are fouling much faster than the design assumptions. We scheduled cleaning cycles every two weeks, but in practice the operators are forced to do a full CIP clean every five to seven days because transmembrane pressure spikes. A full CIP uses roughly 200 litres of citric acid and caustic solution per unit and takes the system offline for four to six hours. That adds up to significant chemical cost and lost treatment capacity over a year. We have tried adjusting aeration intensity and sludge retention time, but the fouling rate has not changed much. Dairy wastewater has high fats, proteins, and sugars, and we think the combination is forming a gel layer the biology is not breaking down fast enough. We do not have the tools or know-how to characterise the foulant properly. Our service records go back three years and show a clear seasonal pattern — fouling is worst in summer, which might point to temperature effects on the biology or on the fat chemistry. A good outcome would be a reliable explanation of what is causing the fouling and a practical change — to pre-treatment, aeration, or membrane material — that pushes cleaning intervals back to at least twelve days.
